claim: A minimal branched actin network is sufficient to internalize endocytic pits against membrane tension.
source: An experimentally constrained multiscale model shows that a minimal branched actin network is sufficient to internalize endocytic pits against membrane tension.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 1 and described in the Results section.

claim: Around 200 activated Arp2/3 complexes are required for robust internalization.
source: Around 200 activated Arp2/3 complexes are required for robust internalization.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by simulations shown in Figure 1G and molecule counting experiments shown in Figure 2I.

claim: ~200 Arp2/3 complexes assemble at sites of clathrin-mediated endocytosis in human cells.
source: A newly developed molecule-counting method determined that ~200 Arp2/3 complexes assemble at sites of clathrin-mediated endocytosis in human cells.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 2I using a newly developed molecule counting method.

claim: Actin self-organizes into a radial branched array with growing ends oriented toward the base of the pit.
source: Simulations predict that actin self-organizes into a radial branched array with growing ends oriented toward the base of the pit.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by simulation results shown in Figure 3.

claim: Long actin filaments bend between attachment sites in the coat and the base of the pit.
source: Long actin filaments bend between attachment sites in the coat and the base of the pit.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by simulation results in Figure 5A and cryo-electron tomography in Figure 5B.

claim: Elastic energy stored in bent filaments contributes to endocytic internalization.
source: Elastic energy stored in bent filaments, whose presence was confirmed by cryo-electron tomography, contributes to endocytic internalization.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by simulation results in Figure 5F-I showing energy storage and release.

claim: Elevated membrane tension directs more growing filaments toward the base of the pit.
source: Elevated membrane tension directs more growing filaments toward the base of the pit, increasing actin nucleation and bending for increased force production.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by simulation results in Figure 7F showing increased barbed ends near the base under higher tension.

claim: Elevated membrane tension increases actin nucleation for increased force production.
source: Elevated membrane tension directs more growing filaments toward the base of the pit, increasing actin nucleation and bending for increased force production.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by simulation results in Figure 7G showing increased filament numbers under higher tension.

claim: Elevated membrane tension increases actin filament bending for increased force production.
source: Elevated membrane tension directs more growing filaments toward the base of the pit, increasing actin nucleation and bending for increased force production.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by simulation results in Figure 7H showing increased bending energy under higher tension.

claim: Branched actin networks drive the plasma membrane forward during cell migration on a large (µm) length scale.
source: On a large (µm) length scale, branched actin networks drive the plasma membrane forward during cell migration, such that on the scale of individual actin branches, the membrane shape can be thought of as more or less constant (Keren et al., 2008; Mueller et al., 2017; Schaus et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: On a smaller (sub-micron) length scale, branched actin networks deform many cellular membranes as part of organelle and vesicle biogenesis and function.
source: However, on a smaller (sub-micron) length scale, branched actin networks deform many cellular membranes as part of organelle and vesicle biogenesis and function (Rottner et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Clathrin and its adaptor proteins establish a coat that generates initial membrane curvature.
source: Clathrin and its adaptor proteins establish a coat that generates initial membrane curvature (Chen et al., 1998; Pearse, 1976; Stachowiak et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: BAR-domain proteins bind curved membranes and support further membrane curvature.
source: BAR (bin-amphiphysin-rvs)-domain proteins bind curved membranes and support further membrane curvature (Buser and Drubin, 2013; David et al., 1996; Kishimoto et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: During yeast endocytosis, branched actin filaments provide the force required for membrane tubule formation.
source: During yeast endocytosis, branched actin filaments provide the force required for membrane tubule formation (Engqvist-Goldstein and Drubin, 2003; Idrissi et al., 2012; Kukulski et al., 2012; Picco et al., 2018; Sun et al., 2006; Wang and Carlsson, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: In metazoan cells, endocytic pits under high tension stall at a 'U'-shaped intermediate in the absence of functional actin.
source: In metazoan cells, endocytic pits under high tension stall at a 'U'-shaped intermediate in the absence of functional actin (Boulant et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Actin is required to generate plasma membrane shape changes late in CME.
source: In metazoan cells, endocytic pits under high tension stall at a 'U'-shaped intermediate in the absence of functional actin (Boulant et al., 2011), implying that actin is required to generate plasma membrane shape changes late in CME (Hassinger et al., 2017; Yarar et al., 2005; Yoshida et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature and inference from the stalling observation.

claim: A clathrin-coated pit experiences a nearly linear force-extension relationship until an internalization of ~100 nm.
source: Simulations demonstrated that a clathrin-coated pit experiences a nearly linear force-extension relationship until an internalization of ~100 nm, at which point the pit can also adopt a pinched (or 'omega') shape, which requires a lower force (Figure 1C and Figure 1—video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The resistance to internalization is directly proportional to plasma membrane tension for a wide range of coat rigidities.
source: We calculated the resistance to internalization as the slope of the force-extension plot for the linear regime and found that it is directly proportional to plasma membrane tension for a wide range of coat rigidities (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 1D.

claim: This minimal branched actin network internalizes endocytic pits up to ~60 nm against physiological membrane tension.
source: Stochastic simulations of the model showed that this minimal branched actin network internalizes endocytic pits up to ~60 nm against physiological membrane tension (Figure 1F and Figure 1—video 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The extent of internalization is robust to a wide range of parameters, including filament stiffness, stall force, and affinity between Hip1R attachments and actin filaments.
source: We found that the extent of internalization is robust to a wide range of parameters, including filament stiffness, stall force, and affinity between Hip1R attachments and actin filaments (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by parameter sweep results shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The extent of internalization was particularly sensitive to the number of available Arp2/3 complexes.
source: The extent of internalization was particularly sensitive to the number of available Arp2/3 complexes (Figure 1G), indicating a need for precise measurements of this molecule at mammalian endocytic sites.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The fluorescence intensity per spot was unitary and directly proportional to the predicted numbers of molecules per structure (R2 = 0.996).
source: After correcting for exposure time (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E–F), uneven illumination intensity, and local background (Materials and methods), the fluorescence intensity per spot was unitary (Figure 2C) and directly proportional to the predicted numbers of molecules per structure (R2 = 0.996) (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by calibration curve data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The vast majority (81 ± 10%, n = 136) of CME events marked by AP2-RFP culminated in a burst of ArpC3-GFP fluorescence, prior to internalization of the pit.
source: The vast majority (81 ± 10%, n = 136) of CME events marked by AP2-RFP culminated in a burst of ArpC3-GFP fluorescence, prior to internalization of the pit, persisting until the pit internalized (Figure 2G and Figure 2—video 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: 24 ± 4% of ArpC3-GFP tracks (n = 145) did not colocalize with AP2.
source: In addition, 24 ± 4% of ArpC3-GFP tracks (n = 145) did not colocalize with AP2.
evidence: This claim is supported by tracking data from time-lapse imaging experiments.

claim: ~200 molecules of Arp2/3 complex accumulate at clathrin-mediated endocytosis sites over time.
source: Thus, we determined that ~200 molecules of Arp2/3 complex accumulate at clathrin-mediated endocytosis sites over time (Figure 2I).
evidence: This claim is supported by molecule counting data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: This self-organized network drove the assembly of 150 ± 30 actin filaments containing 5700 ± 1100 monomers.
source: This self-organized network drove the assembly of 150 ± 30 actin filaments (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) containing 5700 ± 1100 monomers (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: Only a small number of actin filaments (<5) grew at any given time because the filaments became capped soon after they were nucleated.
source: Interestingly, only a small number of actin filaments (<5) grew at any given time because the filaments became capped soon after they were nucleated (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C; Berro et al., 2010; Rangamani et al., 2011; Xiong et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and citations to published literature.

claim: Filament lengths were exponentially distributed with a final length of 90 ± 80 nm.
source: Filament lengths were exponentially distributed with a final length of 90 ± 80 nm (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D-E.

claim: Actin filaments bound to 120 ± 10 Hip1R molecules in the coat.
source: Actin filaments bound to 120 ± 10 Hip1R molecules in the coat (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The endocytic pit internalized ~60 nm in 10–15 s.
source: The endocytic pit internalized ~60 nm in 10–15 s (Figure 3A and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 3A and D.

claim: Branched actin filaments self-organized into a radial dendritic network with the pointed (minus) ends localized close to the pit and the barbed (plus) ends near the base of the pit oriented to grow toward the base of the pit.
source: Based on the initial geometry of the endocytic pit and activated Arp2/3 complex, branched actin filaments self-organized into a radial dendritic network: the network attached to the clathrin coat by binding to Hip1R, the pointed (minus) ends localized close to the pit and the barbed (plus) ends near the base of the pit were oriented to grow toward the base of the pit (Figure 3A–C and Figure 3—video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 3A-C.

claim: More barbed filament ends localize near the base (10 ± 4 ends) than near the neck of the endocytic pit (1 ± 1 ends).
source: An important consequence of this self-organization is that, based on the position of Hip1R and the Arp2/3 complex, more barbed filament ends localize near the base (10 ± 4 ends) than near the neck of the endocytic pit (1 ± 1 ends) (Figure 3H).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 3H.

claim: An actin network self-organized as described here will produce an axial force during pit internalization.
source: These data result in an important prediction from our model: an actin network self-organized as described here will produce an axial force during pit internalization (Figure 3I).
evidence: This claim is a prediction from the model based on simulation results shown in Figure 3I.

claim: Varying the surface density of Arp2/3 complex along the base of the pit by a factor of 20 had little impact on endocytic outcome.
source: Surprisingly, we found that varying the surface density of Arp2/3 complex along the base of the pit by a factor of 20 had little impact on endocytic outcome (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Localizing some of the active Arp2/3 complex near the neck of the pit did not have an impact on the outcome of simulations (p>0.5).
source: We found that localizing some of the active Arp2/3 complex near the neck of the pit did not have an impact on the outcome of simulations (p>0.5) (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D–E; Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2 with statistical comparison.

claim: The surface distribution of Hip1R around the endocytic pit strongly impacted endocytic outcome.
source: We next conducted a series of simulations in which we varied the surface distribution of a constant number of Hip1R molecules to cover between 1% (localized to the tip of the pit) and 80% (up to the neck of the pit) of the pit (Figure 4B) and found that the surface distribution of Hip1R around the endocytic pit strongly impacted endocytic outcome (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 4.

claim: Both the rate and extent of internalization increased with increasing surface area of Hip1R around the pit.
source: Simulations in each of these conditions revealed that endocytic internalization depends on the surface distribution of actin-coat attachments around the endocytic site (Figure 4C and Figure 4—video 1). Both the rate and extent of internalization increased with increasing surface area of Hip1R around the pit (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Increased Hip1R surface coverage around the pit drove more barbed ends toward the base of the pit.
source: From a functional standpoint, increased Hip1R surface coverage around the pit drove more barbed ends toward the base of the pit (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Increase in Hip1R surface coverage resulted in an increase in Arp2/3 complexes bound in the endocytic actin network.
source: This increase in Hip1R surface coverage resulted in an increase in Arp2/3 complexes bound in the endocytic actin network (Figure 4F), which in turn nucleated more actin filaments (Figure 4G).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 4F.

claim: A threshold of ~100 Hip1R molecules on the pit is necessary for endocytic internalization.
source: Simulations showed that a threshold of ~100 Hip1R molecules on the pit is necessary for endocytic internalization (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Long actin filaments bend between their attachment sites in the clathrin coat and the base of the pit as a result of assembly confined by the membrane at the base of the pit.
source: Closer examination of the simulations revealed that long actin filaments bend between their attachment sites in the clathrin coat and the base of the pit as a result of assembly confined by the membrane at the base of the pit (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Bent actin filaments are present at sites of clathrin-mediated endocytosis in SK-MEL-2 cells.
source: To test the prediction that actin filaments bend at sites of mammalian endocytosis, we used cryo-electron tomography on intact vitrified mammalian (SK-MEL-2) cells. SK-MEL-2 cells grown on electron-microscopy grids are thin at their periphery (<1 µm), which makes them suitable for electron tomography studies. Indeed, we found bent actin filaments present at sites of clathrin-mediated endocytosis, between the clathrin coat (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) and the base of the pit (Figure 5B and Figure 5—video 1), in extended 'U'-shaped clathrin-coated pits similar to the stage modeled in our simulations (Figure 5C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by cryo-electron tomography data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Many (13 ± 3%) of the actin filaments bend further than can be accounted for by thermal fluctuations.
source: We first quantified the filament bending in simulations and found that many (13 ± 3%) of the actin filaments bend further than can be accounted for by thermal fluctuations (Boal and Boal, 2012; Mogilner and Oster, 1996; Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 5E and citations to theoretical work.

claim: Most (92%) of the bent filaments bent less than the minimum energy expected to sever the filaments.
source: Most (92%) of the bent filaments bent less than the minimum energy expected to sever the filaments (De La Cruz et al., 2015b; Sept and McCammon, 2001; Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 5E and citations to published literature.

claim: The bent filaments stored elastic energy by collectively continuing to bend over time, storing up to ~750 pN·nm of elastic energy -- mostly in capped filaments.
source: Importantly, the bent filaments stored elastic energy by collectively continuing to bend over time, storing up to ~750 pN·nm of elastic energy -- mostly in capped filaments (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The amount of elastic energy stored was larger than the magnitude of work required to internalize endocytic pits.
source: In the context of pit internalization, the amount of elastic energy stored was larger than the magnitude of work required to internalize endocytic pits (Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The elastic energy stored in bent filaments was ~1% of the total energy required to polymerize the endocytic actin network.
source: The elastic energy stored in bent filaments was ~1% of the total energy required to polymerize the endocytic actin network (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C–D)
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C-D.

claim: Pit internalization constituted ~0.5% of the total energy from actin filament assembly.
source: with pit internalization constituting ~0.5% of the total energy from actin filament assembly (Figure 5—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2E.

claim: The majority (62 ± 20%) of filament bending energy came from filaments directly bound to Hip1R.
source: The majority (62 ± 20%) of filament bending energy came from filaments directly bound to Hip1R, and 78 ± 25% of the bending energy came from filaments with barbed ends > 5 nm from the coat surface (Figure 5—figure supplement 2F–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2F-H.

claim: 17 ± 16% of bending energy came from filaments with barbed ends near the base of the pit.
source: 17 ± 16% of bending energy came from filaments with barbed ends near the base of the pit (Figure 5—figure supplement 2I).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2I.

claim: Once membrane tension decreases, pit internalization sharply increases.
source: We found that once membrane tension decreases, pit internalization sharply increases (Figure 5H and Figure 5—video 2) and filament bending near the base of the pit gradually decreases by 50% with wide variance (Figure 5I).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Filament bending near the base of the pit gradually decreases by 50% with wide variance after tension is released.
source: We found that once membrane tension decreases, pit internalization sharply increases (Figure 5H and Figure 5—video 2) and filament bending near the base of the pit gradually decreases by 50% with wide variance (Figure 5I).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 5I.

claim: Inhibiting Arp2/3 complex activity stalls endocytosis.
source: Our simulations, conducted by varying the nucleation rate of Arp2/3 complex, predicted that inhibiting Arp2/3 complex activity stalls endocytosis (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 6A-B and experimental validation in Figure 6C-D.

claim: Endocytosis was inhibited when Arp2/3 complex nucleation rates fell below the basal value of 1 filament per second.
source: Endocytosis was inhibited when Arp2/3 complex nucleation rates fell below the basal value of 1 filament per second (Beltzner and Pollard, 2008), and was insensitive to increased rates of nucleation (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 6B and a citation to published literature.

claim: Treatment of SK-MEL-2 cells with CK-666 inhibited endocytic progression in a dose-dependent and time-dependent manner.
source: Treatment of SK-MEL-2 cells with CK-666 inhibited endocytic progression, as marked by the lifetimes of endogenously tagged AP2-RFP or dynamin2-GFP at endocytic sites, in a dose-dependent and time-dependent manner (Figure 6C–D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C-D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Endocytic progression attenuated in a tension-dependent manner.
source: In our simulations, endocytic progression attenuated in a tension-dependent manner (Figure 7A–E), consistent with previous modeling (Hassinger et al., 2017) and experimental observations (Boulant et al., 2011; Ferguson et al., 2017; Ferguson et al., 2016; Wu et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 7A-E and citations to published literature.

claim: At higher membrane tensions, endocytosis persisted better than expected for a non-adapting network.
source: However, at higher membrane tensions, endocytosis persisted better than expected for a non-adapting network, suggesting the existence of an adaptive mechanism (Figure 7E).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 7E comparing to a non-adapting baseline.

claim: Under low tension (0.015 pN/nm), endocytic pits internalize strongly and few barbed ends encounter the base of the pit.
source: We found that under low tension (0.015 pN/nm), endocytic pits internalize strongly (Figure 7B and E) and few barbed ends encounter the base of the pit (Figure 7F), with fewer Arp2/3 complexes recruited to the network (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A) and a correspondingly low filament bending energy (Figure 7H).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 7B, E, F, H and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Under >50 x higher membrane tension (1 pN/nm), endocytic internalization slowed but was not abolished.
source: Under >50 x higher membrane tension (1 pN/nm), endocytic internalization slowed but was not abolished (Figure 7E).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Under high tension, more barbed ends encountered the base of the pit, binding more Arp2/3 complexes to nucleate more actin filaments and increasing the total actin filament bending energy near the base of the pit.
source: For these pits, more barbed ends encountered the base of the pit (Figure 7F), binding more Arp2/3 complexes (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A) to nucleate more actin filaments (Figure 7G) and increasing the total actin filament bending energy near the base of the pit (Figure 7H).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 7F, G, H and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Upon increasing membrane tension, the overall endocytic energy efficiency increased.
source: As a result, upon increasing membrane tension, the overall endocytic energy efficiency increased (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Cells with high membrane tension are especially sensitive to changes in Arp2/3 complex nucleation rate.
source: This phase diagram shows that cells with high membrane tension are especially sensitive to changes in Arp2/3 complex nucleation rate (Kaplan et al., in preparation), whereas cells with low membrane tension carry out endocytosis even with low Arp2/3 complex activity, consistent with experimental observations (Boulant et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by the phase diagram shown in Figure 8B and citations to published and unpublished work.

claim: Cells with low membrane tension carry out endocytosis even with low Arp2/3 complex activity.
source: This phase diagram shows that cells with high membrane tension are especially sensitive to changes in Arp2/3 complex nucleation rate (Kaplan et al., in preparation), whereas cells with low membrane tension carry out endocytosis even with low Arp2/3 complex activity, consistent with experimental observations (Boulant et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by the phase diagram shown in Figure 8B and a citation to published literature.

claim: The endocytic actin network's ability to adapt to load depends on Hip1R coverage around the pit.
source: We found that the endocytic actin network's ability to adapt to load (Figure 7) depends on Hip1R coverage around the pit (Figure 8D–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 8D-F.

claim: As the coverage of Hip1R around the pit increased, actin's ability to adapt to changes in membrane tension also increased.
source: As the coverage of Hip1R around the pit increased, actin's ability to adapt to changes in membrane tension also increased, as measured by the number of barbed ends near the base of the pit (Figure 8D), the binding of active Arp2/3 complex at the base of the pit (Figure 8E), subsequent nucleation of additional actin filaments (Figure 8F), and bending of actin filaments near the base of the pit (Figure 8G).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 8D-G.

claim: Approximately 200 Arp2/3 complexes constitutively assemble at sites of endocytosis in human induced pluripotent stem cells.
source: Approximately 200 Arp2/3 complexes constitutively assemble at sites of endocytosis in human induced pluripotent stem cells.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion and supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Endocytic actin filaments self-organize into a radial dendritic array, in which filaments grow toward the base of the pit.
source: Endocytic actin filaments self-organize into a radial dendritic array, in which filaments grow toward the base of the pit.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion and supported by simulation results shown in Figure 3.

claim: These filaments bend and store elastic energy, which supports internalization.
source: These filaments bend and store elastic energy, which supports internalization.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion and supported by simulation results shown in Figure 5.

claim: The endocytic actin network adapts to changes in membrane tension by driving more filaments to the base of the pit and increasing filament bending.
source: The endocytic actin network adapts to changes in membrane tension by driving more filaments to the base of the pit and increasing filament bending, which supports a higher load and nucleates more actin filaments.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion and supported by simulation results shown in Figure 7 and Figure 8.

claim: Knocking down Hip1R in HeLa cells inhibited endocytosis.
source: Previous experiments from our lab showed that knocking down Hip1R in HeLa cells inhibited endocytosis (Engqvist-Goldstein et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature from the authors' lab.

claim: Capping actin filament elongation with the small molecule compound Cytochalasin inhibits CME.
source: Second, experiments showed that capping actin filament elongation with the small molecule compound Cytochalasin inhibits CME, reflected by an increase in stalled endocytic sites marked by clathrin-RFP (Brady et al., 2010) or slower accumulation of dynamin2-GFP at endocytic sites (Grassart et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The spatial segregation of Arp2/3 complex activation and Hip1R linker proteins on the clathrin coat are important factors for effective force generation.
source: First, we found that the spatial segregation of Arp2/3 complex activation and Hip1R linker proteins on the clathrin coat are important factors for effective force generation.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion and supported by simulation results shown in Figure 4.

claim: Based on the relative positions of Arp2/3 complex activators and actin filament linkers, the resultant self-organized actin network orients to produce force orthogonal to the base of the pit rather than producing a pinching force on the neck.
source: We conclude that based on the relative positions of Arp2/3 complex activators and actin filament linkers, the resultant self-organized actin network orients to produce force orthogonal to the base of the pit rather than producing a pinching force on the neck (Collins et al., 2011; Hassinger et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion and supported by simulation results shown in Figure 3I and citations to published literature.

claim: The effective anchoring of actin filaments to the surface of the pit depends on the distribution of linker proteins on the pit surface.
source: Second, the effective anchoring of actin filaments to the surface of the pit depends on the distribution of linker proteins on the pit surface.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion and supported by simulation results shown in Figure 4.

claim: One possible function of a large coat is for the actin-linking proteins Hip1, Hip1R and Epsin to cover enough surface area to provide leverage for internalization.
source: This observation suggests that one possible function of a large coat is for the actin-linking proteins Hip1, Hip1R and Epsin to cover enough surface area to provide leverage for internalization.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion and is an inference from simulation results shown in Figure 4.

claim: Bent filaments might contribute to the resilience of endocytosis by preventing backsliding of the pit.
source: We predict that the bent filaments, whose existence we confirmed by cryo-electron tomography of intact cells, contribute to successful endocytic internalization in at least two ways. First, they might contribute to the resilience of endocytosis by preventing backsliding of the pit.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion and is a prediction based on simulation results shown in Figure 5.

claim: Bent filaments contribute to internalization by releasing stored elastic energy when they straighten out under thermal fluctuations, consistent with the elastic Brownian ratchet mechanism for actin-mediated force production.
source: Second, we expect that they contribute to internalization by releasing stored elastic energy when they straighten out under thermal fluctuations, consistent with the elastic Brownian ratchet mechanism for actin-mediated force production (De La Cruz and Gardel, 2015a; Mogilner and Oster, 1996).
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion and is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 5 and citations to published literature.

claim: Filament bending occurs to a greater extent and for a longer time than previously described for coherent flat surfaces like the leading edge, possibly due to the curved geometry of endocytic pits.
source: Here, filament bending occurs to a greater extent and for a longer time than previously described for coherent flat surfaces like the leading edge, possibly due to the curved geometry of endocytic pits.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion and is an inference from simulation results shown in Figure 5.

claim: The distribution of Hip1R linkers around the pit directs more filaments to grow toward the base of the pit, which nucleates more filaments autocatalytically and increases filament bending, thereby supporting greater internalization.
source: Here, the distribution of Hip1R linkers around the pit directs more filaments to grow toward the base of the pit (Figure 4), which nucleates more filaments autocatalytically and increases filament bending (Figure 5), thereby supporting greater internalization (Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion and supported by simulation results shown in Figures 4, 5, and 7.

claim: An agent-based model of endocytic actin networks in yeast predicted that barbed filament ends radiate away from the center of pit in the XY plane.
source: An agent-based model of endocytic actin networks in yeast predicted that barbed filament ends radiate away from the center of pit in the XY plane (Mund et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The >200 x larger force requirements in yeast lead to a different axial organization of the filaments, less filament bending, and a distinct mechanism of force production sufficient to counteract high turgor pressure.
source: However, the >200 x larger force requirements in this organism lead to a different axial organization of the filaments, less filament bending, and a distinct mechanism of force production sufficient to counteract high turgor pressure.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion and is an inference comparing the current work to published work on yeast.

claim: Single-particle electron microscopy reconstructions and the crystal structure (PDB: 2p9l) of Arp2/3 complex show that the C terminus of ArpC3 is flexible and does not sterically interfere with Arp2/3 complex's binding site to actin filaments or its activators (VCA).
source: Single-particle electron microscopy reconstructions and the crystal structure (PDB: 2p9l) of Arp2/3 complex show that the C terminus of ArpC3 is flexible and does not sterically interfere with Arp2/3 complex's binding site to actin filaments or its activators (VCA).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to structural data.

claim: Cells tagged at both alleles of the ArpC3 gene had twice the fluorescence intensity of cells with a single allele tagged.
source: Cells tagged at both alleles of the ArpC3 gene had twice the fluorescence intensity of cells with a single allele tagged, suggesting direct proportionality between GFP fluorescence intensity and numbers of molecules (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C-D.

claim: The branching angle of Arp2/3 complex is 77 ± 13°, as measured for bovine Arp2/3 complex.
source: Based on Blanchoin et al. (2000) we set the branching angle of Arp2/3 complex to be 77 ± 13°, as measured for bovine Arp2/3 complex.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: In NIH3T3 cells preserved by cryo-fixation, branch angles in the lamellipodium are 77 ± 8°.
source: In NIH3T3 cells preserved by cryo-fixation, branch angles in the lamellipodium are 77 ± 8° (Vinzenz et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The cytoplasmic concentration of actin is 60–100 µM.
source: In cells the cytoplasmic concentration of actin is 60–100 µM (Haugwitz et al., 1994; Wu and Pollard, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The association rate constant of ATP-actin is 11.6 subunits/µM/s.
source: We conservatively set the concentration of available polymerizable actin to be 20 µM, which given the association rate constant of ATP-actin of 11.6 subunits/µM/s (Pollard, 1986) corresponds to a polymerization rate of 500 nm (182 subunits) per second.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The persistence length of actin filaments is 10 µm, which corresponds to a flexural rigidity of 0.041 pN·µm2.
source: We set the persistence length of actin filaments to be 10 µm, which corresponds to a flexural rigidity of 0.041 pN·µm2 (McCullough et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Phalloidin stiffens actin filaments.
source: Previous modeling studies used a value of 20 µm, based on measurements of actin filaments labeled with phalloidin (Gittes et al., 1993), which stiffens actin filaments (Isambert et al., 1995; Pfaendtner et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.
